facts.one_liner: Powder-white sand and impossibly clear turquoise water along Providenciales’ north shore.
facts.why_go: Grace Bay stretches for miles along the north coast of Providenciales and regularly tops lists of the world’s best beaches. A barrier reef offshore, protected within Princess Alexandra National Park, keeps the water calm and clear for snorkelling and paddleboarding, and the sand stays soft and uncrowded even with resorts behind it.
facts.best_time: December–April for dry, breezy weather; hurricane season runs June–November.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Providenciales International Airport (PLS), about 15–20 minutes by taxi from Grace Bay.
facts.good_to_know: Public access paths run between the resorts. Snorkel at Bight Reef (Coral Gardens) at the western end.

facts.one_liner: Black volcanic sand, hexagonal basalt columns and the Reynisdrangar sea stacks near Vík.
facts.why_go: Reynisfjara on Iceland’s south coast is a wild black-sand beach backed by towering basalt columns on the slopes of Reynisfjall. Offshore rise the jagged Reynisdrangar sea stacks, said in folklore to be trolls caught by daylight. Puffins nest on the cliffs in summer, and the roaring Atlantic surf makes it one of Iceland’s most dramatic sights.
facts.best_time: June–August for long days and puffins; winter for moody light and the chance of northern lights.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 2.5 hours’ drive east of Reykjavík along Route 1, then a short side road just west of Vík.
facts.good_to_know: Sneaker waves here are deadly: stay well back from the water and follow the warning-light system at the entrance.

facts.one_liner: A shallow turquoise lagoon and pink-tinged sand on Crete’s far south-west corner.
facts.why_go: Elafonissi is a protected beach and islet on the south-western tip of Crete, famed for sand tinted pink by crushed shells and a shallow lagoon you can wade across to the islet. Part of a Natura 2000 site, its dunes and juniper scrub are fragile, so visitors stick to marked paths.
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October for warm water without peak crowds.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 1.5–2 hours’ drive from Chania; summer buses run from Chania bus station.
facts.good_to_know: Do not take any pink sand—it is protected. Arrive early in summer for parking.

facts.one_liner: A lunar landscape of wind-carved white volcanic rock around a deep blue inlet.
facts.why_go: Sarakiniko, on the north coast of Milos, is famous for its brilliant white, wave-sculpted volcanic rock that looks like the surface of the moon. A narrow inlet of deep blue water cuts through the rock, and the small sandy cove and old mining tunnels make it a favourite for swimming and photography.
facts.best_time: June–September for swimming; sunrise or sunset for soft light and fewer people.
facts.how_to_get_there: Ferries and flights reach Milos from Athens; Sarakiniko is about 10 minutes’ drive from the port of Adamas.
facts.good_to_know: There is no shade—bring water and sun protection. Rocks can be slippery near the water.

facts.one_liner: Kilometres of golden sand beneath layered red and ochre cliffs.
facts.why_go: Praia da Falésia runs for about six kilometres between Olhos de Água and Vilamoura, backed by striking cliffs streaked red, orange and white and topped with umbrella pines. Its long, wide sand makes it one of the Algarve’s best beaches for walks and sunsets.
facts.best_time: May–October for beach weather; spring and autumn are quieter.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 30 minutes’ drive from Faro Airport; nearest towns are Albufeira and Vilamoura.
facts.good_to_know: Stay back from the cliff edges and bases—they are soft and can collapse.

facts.one_liner: A golden sea cave with a round skylight open to the sky, reached from the sea.
facts.why_go: The Algar de Benagil is a vast sea cave in the limestone cliffs near the fishing village of Benagil. A circular opening in its domed roof floods the hidden beach inside with light, creating one of Portugal’s most photographed natural wonders.
facts.best_time: April–October, mornings for calmer seas and fewer boats.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 50 minutes’ drive from Faro; boat, kayak and paddleboard tours leave from Benagil and nearby Carvoeiro and Portimão.
facts.good_to_know: Since 2024, rules limit access and landing on the cave beach—book a licensed tour and check current regulations.

facts.one_liner: A white crescent of sand linking two of the car-free Cíes Islands.
facts.why_go: Playa de Rodas is the curving sandbar that joins Monteagudo and Faro islands in the Cíes archipelago, part of the Atlantic Islands of Galicia National Park. Its calm, crystal water and fine white sand once earned it the title of the world’s best beach from The Guardian.
facts.best_time: Mid-May to September, when ferries run; July–August is busiest.
facts.how_to_get_there: Ferries from Vigo, Baiona and Cangas take 30–45 minutes; you need a free authorisation from the Xunta de Galicia in addition to a ferry ticket.
facts.good_to_know: Daily visitor numbers are capped. Water is Atlantic-cold even in summer.

facts.one_liner: One of Mallorca’s last undeveloped beaches: dunes, pines and clear shallow water.
facts.why_go: Es Trenc on Mallorca’s south coast is a long, natural beach of fine white sand backed by dunes and salt flats, all within a protected natural area. There are no hotels on the beach itself, and its shallow, turquoise water feels almost Caribbean.
facts.best_time: June and September for warm water and fewer crowds.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 45 minutes’ drive from Palma; parking areas at Ses Covetes and Colònia de Sant Jordi.
facts.good_to_know: Facilities are limited; bring water and shade. Visit the Salines d’Es Trenc salt pans nearby.

facts.one_liner: Shallow, glassy water beside an Aragonese watchtower on Sardinia’s north-west tip.
facts.why_go: La Pelosa near Stintino is one of Italy’s most beautiful beaches, with fine white sand and shallow, transparent water guarded by the 16th-century Torre della Pelosa on its islet. The island of Asinara, a national park, lies just offshore.
facts.best_time: June and September for warm sea and smaller crowds.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 1 hour’s drive from Alghero or Sassari; Stintino is the nearest village.
facts.good_to_know: Daily access in summer is capped and must be booked online for a small fee; towel mats are required to protect the sand.

facts.one_liner: A turquoise cove facing a tiny island, nesting ground of loggerhead turtles.
facts.why_go: Spiaggia dei Conigli on Lampedusa, Italy’s southernmost island, faces the tiny Isola dei Conigli across a shallow channel of brilliant blue water. It is part of a nature reserve where loggerhead sea turtles nest, and it has been voted among the best beaches in the world.
facts.best_time: June and September; part of the beach is closed at night in summer during turtle nesting season.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly or ferry to Lampedusa (from Palermo, Catania or Porto Empedocle); the beach is about 15 minutes from town by scooter or bus.
facts.good_to_know: Visitor numbers are managed in summer. Bring shade; follow reserve rules.

facts.one_liner: A brilliant white marl cliff stepped like a giant staircase above the sea.
facts.why_go: Scala dei Turchi (‘Stair of the Turks’) is a gleaming white cliff of marl near Realmonte on Sicily’s south coast, eroded into natural steps. The beaches on either side look up at it, and it glows at sunset. It is just a short drive from the ancient Valley of the Temples.
facts.best_time: May–October; late afternoon for golden light on the cliff.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 20 minutes’ drive west of Agrigento.
facts.good_to_know: Climbing on the cliff itself has been restricted to protect it—admire it from the beach.

facts.one_liner: Umbrella pines, red granite and turquoise water on Corsica’s south-east coast.
facts.why_go: Palombaggia, south of Porto-Vecchio, is often called Corsica’s most beautiful beach: soft pale sand fringed with umbrella pines and pink-red granite boulders, looking out to the Cerbicale Islands nature reserve.
facts.best_time: June and September for warm water and quieter sands.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 20 minutes’ drive south of Porto-Vecchio; Figari airport is about 30 minutes away.
facts.good_to_know: Parking fills early in July–August. Several beach restaurants serve lunch.

facts.one_liner: A pebble cove hidden behind a narrow gap in towering cliffs on the island of Vis.
facts.why_go: Stiniva on the south coast of Vis is a small pebble beach enclosed by high limestone cliffs that almost meet at the entrance, leaving a narrow gap to the open sea. Reached by boat or a steep path, it feels like a secret amphitheatre of rock and turquoise water.
facts.best_time: June–September; go early or late to avoid boat crowds.
facts.how_to_get_there: Ferries and catamarans from Split reach Vis in 1.5–2.5 hours; Stiniva is best visited by boat from Vis town or Komiža.
facts.good_to_know: The footpath down is steep and rocky—wear good shoes. Boat entry may be restricted in summer.

facts.one_liner: Turquoise shallows dotted with tiny islands on Albania’s southern coast.
facts.why_go: Ksamil, on the Albanian Riviera close to the Greek border, is known for its clear turquoise water and small wooded islands you can swim or paddle to. It is a short drive from the ancient city of Butrint, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
facts.best_time: June and September for warm water without the July–August crowds.
facts.how_to_get_there: Ferries run from Corfu to Sarandë (30–75 minutes); Ksamil is about 20 minutes’ drive south.
facts.good_to_know: Many beaches are lined with paid sunbeds. Visit Butrint in the morning before heat sets in.

facts.one_liner: A tiny cove of brilliant blue water at the foot of a gorge between Kaş and Kalkan.
facts.why_go: Kaputaş Beach sits at the mouth of a narrow gorge on the Lycian coast between Kaş and Kalkan. Steps lead down from the coastal road to a small strip of sand and water of an intense turquoise blue, set against steep mountain slopes.
facts.best_time: May–October; mornings for calmer water and easier parking.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 20 minutes’ drive from Kaş or Kalkan; dolmuş minibuses stop at the top of the steps.
facts.good_to_know: There are around 180 steps down; facilities are basic.

facts.one_liner: Turquoise water and serpentine rock islands on the Lizard Peninsula.
facts.why_go: Kynance Cove, owned by the National Trust, is one of Cornwall’s most celebrated beaches: white sand, dark serpentine rock stacks and islands, and water that turns brilliant turquoise on sunny days. At low tide you can explore caves and sandbars between the islands.
facts.best_time: May–September at low tide; spring for wildflowers on the clifftops.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 20 minutes’ drive south of Helston; National Trust car park then a 15-minute walk down.
facts.good_to_know: Check tide times—the beach largely disappears at high tide.

facts.one_liner: A white-sand cove with Caribbean-blue water beneath the Minack Theatre.
facts.why_go: Porthcurno near Land’s End is a sheltered cove of fine shell sand and turquoise water between granite cliffs. Above it, the open-air Minack Theatre is carved into the cliff, and the PK Porthcurno museum tells how undersea telegraph cables once came ashore here.
facts.best_time: May–September; book a Minack performance on a summer evening.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 20 minutes’ drive from Penzance; buses run from Penzance.
facts.good_to_know: Swimming can have strong currents—use lifeguarded areas in season.

facts.one_liner: Wide golden sands and dunes beneath the walls of Bamburgh Castle.
facts.why_go: Bamburgh Beach is a broad sweep of sand and dunes on the Northumberland Coast, dominated by Bamburgh Castle on its basalt crag. From the beach you can see the Farne Islands, famous for puffins and seals, and Holy Island (Lindisfarne) to the north.
facts.best_time: May–July for puffin boat trips from Seahouses; year-round for bracing walks.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 1 hour’s drive north of Newcastle; Chathill and Berwick are the nearest stations.
facts.good_to_know: The North Sea is cold—wetsuit recommended. The castle is open to visitors most of the year.

facts.one_liner: Powder-soft quartz sand that stays cool underfoot on Florida’s Gulf Coast.
facts.why_go: Siesta Key Beach near Sarasota is famous for its sand, made almost entirely of fine quartz, which stays white and cool even in the summer sun. Gentle Gulf waters, colourful lifeguard towers and the Sunday drum circle at sunset make it a classic Florida beach.
facts.best_time: March–May and October–November for warm, less humid weather.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 20 minutes’ drive from Sarasota-Bradenton Airport; a free trolley runs along the key.
facts.good_to_know: Hurricane season is June–November. Parking at the public beach is free but fills on weekends.

facts.one_liner: Pastel lifeguard towers and Art Deco Miami on the Atlantic.
facts.why_go: South Beach is the southern stretch of Miami Beach, where colourful lifeguard towers line the sand and the Art Deco Historic District’s pastel hotels face Ocean Drive. It is a place for people-watching, nightlife and long swims in warm Atlantic water.
facts.best_time: November–April for dry, warm weather.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 25 minutes’ drive from Miami International Airport.
facts.good_to_know: Hurricane season runs June–November. Take an Art Deco walking tour.
